source.title: Cross-Platform Evaluation of Reasoning Capabilities in Foundation Models
source.authors: J. de Curtò; I. de Zarzà; Pablo García; Jordi Cabot

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. It includes extracted figures and tables; some figure values are not numerically available in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates reasoning-benchmark performance across models of different sizes and explicitly argues that these results challenge monotonic scaling assumptions. It does not test pretraining cross-entropy scaling laws or compute-optimal training allocations.
record.gate_note: The study reports benchmark scores for differently sized models, including same-family comparisons, which bear on V6. It does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, sweep training tokens or compute, fit scaling laws, test extrapolation from small runs, or control model architecture and training data in a scaling experiment. Its figures about difficulty tiers and domain performance are not separate scaling-law results.
record.test_reason: The study compares off-the-shelf models of different sizes, including within-family pairs (Hermes-4 70B/405B, Qwen3 30B/235B, GPT-OSS 20B/120B), on a reasoning benchmark. It argues these results challenge scaling assumptions, which bears weakly on V6. The evidence is weak: there is no controlled scale sweep, models differ in post-training, the metric is embedding cosine similarity with a 300-token output cap, and there is no pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors claim reasoning scores no longer scale monotonically with parameter count, with a plateau beyond about 70B and a 'data-limited regime'. They conclude training data quality and architecture matter more than size. Some supporting comparisons are flawed. The Llama 3.3-70B vs 3.1-8B 'regression' mixes the 79-problem and 19-problem sets. Phi-4-mini is misstated as 14B. The Hermes 70B vs 405B gap is non-significant on the 19-problem set.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures cosine similarity of model answers and reasoning steps on academic problems, rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy across controlled parameter, token, or compute sweeps. It does not fit scaling laws or optimize training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary between the 19- and 79-problem benchmarks; the paper reports Phi-4-mini above Phi-3-mini on the 19-problem university-cluster evaluation but slightly below it on the 79-problem evaluation. It also notes software configuration and quantization can affect results, but does not test those variations here.
record.problems: Model sizes are not varied in controlled training sweeps; compared models differ in family, architecture, training data, and training procedure. The outcome is reasoning-benchmark cosine similarity, not pretraining loss. The Hermes-4 70B versus 405B comparison on the 19-problem set is reported as not statistically significant (p = 0.514).
record.rows_left_out: Other benchmark score entries, including the full set of 19-problem university-cluster models and the initial MareNostrum baseline models, were omitted because they do not add a controlled size comparison beyond the reported model and benchmark comparisons. Domain, difficulty-tier, step-accuracy, and consistency results were also omitted because they are not measures of downstream performance versus model scale.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss and no parameter, token or compute sweep.
No other modalities or training regimes.
No link to pretraining loss, no controlled scale sweep, and no fitted trend.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is weak for V6: heterogeneous post-trained models, a semantic-similarity metric and truncated outputs (max 300 tokens), which plausibly hurts reasoning models such as GPT-OSS and DeepSeek-R1. The paper misreports sizes for Phi-4-mini and DeepSeek-R1-0528. The abstract gives Llama 3.1-405B as 0.560 but Table 11 gives 0.569.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss, parameter/token/compute sweep, or power-law fit.
No fits on small runs or comparison of extrapolated predictions with larger runs.
No fixed-compute-budget experiment or parameter/token allocation analysis.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No tests of scaling-law form in other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

Tests reasoning-benchmark scores against model size in a heterogeneous set of models; it does not test whether downstream performance tracks pretraining loss or establish a controlled, general scaling relationship.
No analysis of fitted exponents, parameter-counting or fitting choices, or curvature of fitted loss curves.

rows.subject: NousResearch/Hermes-4-70B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated reasoning-benchmark final score; compared with differently sized models.
rows.note: Highest overall score in the 79-problem Nebius evaluation; the table reports 100.0% coverage.
rows.check: Comparator for r2, not an effect on its own.

rows.subject: NousResearch/Hermes-4-405B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated reasoning-benchmark final score; same family as Hermes-4-70B.
rows.note: The larger Hermes-4 variant scores below the 70B variant.
rows.check: 0.573 vs 0.598 for Hermes-4-70B. The gap is small relative to run-to-run std (0.032) and no significance test is reported for the 79-problem set, so the reversal is weak.

rows.subject: meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated reasoning-benchmark final score across a heterogeneous model cohort.
rows.note: Not a controlled size comparison with the other model families.
rows.check: Llama 3.1-405B vs 3.3-70B are different releases. 405B is slightly higher (0.569 vs 0.561), but the pair is confounded.

rows.subject: meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated reasoning-benchmark final score across a heterogeneous model cohort.
rows.note: The conclusion also reports LLaMA 3.3-70B at 0.561 versus LLaMA 3.1-8B at 0.593, while noting that these are different versions.
rows.check: The paper's 'regression' claim compares 0.561 (79-problem set) with Llama-3.1-8B's 0.593 (MareNostrum 19-problem set), which are different benchmarks. On the same 79-problem set, 3.3-70B (0.561) is slightly above 3.1-8B (0.551, r12).

rows.subject: Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated reasoning-benchmark final score across a heterogeneous model cohort.
rows.note: The text describes Qwen3 scores as stable, mid-tier results; no controlled training-scale sweep is reported.
rows.check: Qwen3-235B is slightly above Qwen3-30B (0.487 vs 0.477): a small move in the scaling direction.

rows.subject: Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507

rows.subject: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-0528
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated reasoning-benchmark final score across a heterogeneous model cohort.
rows.note: The paper reports this score as moderate; its other reported measure, step accuracy, is not a scaling-law measure.
rows.check: Size is wrong: the paper lists 70B, but DeepSeek-R1-0528 is a 671B MoE. It has no same-family size partner, so it is not a scaling comparison.

rows.subject: openai/gpt-oss-20b
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated reasoning-benchmark final score across a heterogeneous model cohort.
rows.note: Coverage was 72.2% (57 problems).
rows.check: Comparator for r9; only 72.2% coverage.

rows.subject: openai/gpt-oss-120b
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated reasoning-benchmark final score across a heterogeneous model cohort.
rows.note: Coverage was 83.5% (66 problems).
rows.check: GPT-OSS-120B 0.404 vs 20B 0.406: no gain. Coverage differs (83.5% vs 72.2%), likely affected by the 300-token cap.

rows.subject: microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated reasoning-benchmark final score across models and compared with Phi variants.
rows.note: The authors report this as slightly higher than Phi-4-mini on the 79-problem set.
rows.check: Phi-3-mini vs Phi-4-mini is a generational comparison, not a scale comparison. Phi-4-mini-instruct is also about 3.8B, not 14B as the paper states.

rows.subject: microsoft/Phi-4-mini-instruct
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated reasoning-benchmark final score across models and compared with Phi variants.

rows.check: Not a scale contrast: the paper misstates Phi-4-mini as 14B, and the difference from Phi-3-mini is non-significant (p = 0.883). Should not be marked reversed.

relationships.condition: Within-family size pairs of post-trained instruct models (Hermes-4 70B/405B, GPT-OSS 20B/120B) on a cosine-similarity reasoning benchmark
relationships.reason: Larger variants show no gain or a slight drop (r2, r18, r9, r25). Hermes-4 19-problem difference non-significant (p = 0.514). Effects are confounded by post-training and a 300-token cap.
relationships.display_finding: Larger variants showed no gain or slight declines; the Hermes-4 difference across 19 problems was nonsignificant at p = 0.514, with post-training and a 300-token cap confounding interpretation.

relationships.reason: The larger Qwen3 scores slightly higher on both problem sets (r5, r21), a small gain in the expected direction.
relationships.display_finding: Qwen3 235B-A22B scored slightly higher than 30B-A3B on both problem sets.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Hermes-4 models on the 19- and 79-problem Nebius evaluations
reader_labels.reason: In both evaluations, Hermes-4-70B scores above Hermes-4-405B (r17–r18 and r1–r2), contrary to predictable improvement with larger size; the reported 19-problem pairwise test is not significant.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Phi variants across the university-cluster 19- and 79-problem benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: The larger Phi-4-mini is above Phi-3-mini on 19 problems but slightly below it on 79 problems (r10–r11, r26–r27); results vary with benchmark, and model generation/training is not controlled.
